hypothesis: The 4-byte keccak256 function selector creates an information-theoretic bottleneck that dominates all ABI recovery methods: because the selector-to-signature mapping is many-to-one and preimage-resistant by design, all methods (static analysis, dynamic analysis, ML, LLM-based) converge on selector *identification* accuracy but diverge irreducibly on *parameter type* recovery, since the latter depends on external knowledge (4byte.directory, verified-source corpora) rather than any bytecode-intrinsic signal.
rationale: SigRec (Chen et al., 2021, IEEE TSE) demonstrates that function selectors can be located via dispatch-pattern analysis — PUSH4 instruction sequences that load selectors and EQ comparisons that match them — without source code. 'Abusing the Ethereum Smart Contract Verification Services for Fun and Profit' (2023) shows that 4byte.directory, the database SigRec and most tools depend on for selector resolution, can be poisoned with misleading entries. Elipmoc (Grech et al., 2022, PACMPL) achieves 99.5% operand resolution but still requires external type knowledge for ABI parameter types. 'Decompiling Smart Contracts with a Large Language Model' (David et al., 2025) and SCDBench (Qin et al., 2026) show LLMs produce plausible but often semantically incorrect signatures — exactly the pattern expected when the model hallucinates beyond what the selector can constrain. The information-theoretic ceiling is 32 bits of selector entropy, which is insufficient to uniquely identify a signature from the infinite Solidity signature space.
supports_if: Experiments show that the precision gap between methods shrinks to near-zero when evaluating only function entry detection (do we find all functions?) but remains large when evaluating parameter-type accuracy (do we get uint256 vs address right?). SCDBench already reports that ABI recovery is an intermediate evaluation stage where LLMs perform better than traditional decompilers at format but stall at semantic consistency — consistent with the selector bottleneck hypothesis.
refutes_if: A method emerges that can correctly resolve the full parameter type list (count, order, and Solidity type) of a significant fraction of functions *without* relying on any external signature database or training data derived from verified source contracts — i.e., purely from bytecode opcode semantics on how parameters are loaded, stored, and used. This would demonstrate that bytecode does carry sufficient intrinsic information to invert the selector, contradicting the bottleneck claim.
motivating_papers: SigRec: Automatic Recovery of Function Signatures in Smart Contracts
Abusing the Ethereum Smart Contract Verification Services for Fun and Profit
Elipmoc: advanced decompilation of Ethereum smart contracts
Decompiling Smart Contracts with a Large Language Model
SCDBench: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Smart Contract Decompilers

hypothesis: Compiler optimization (Solidity's --optimize flag) imposes a monotonically decreasing, irreversible information-loss ceiling on ABI recovery such that no method — static, dynamic, or learning-based — can recover type information that the optimizer has semantically erased, because the Solidity compiler's optimization passes (dead-code elimination, constant folding, instruction reordering) are non-injective transformations that discard source-level ABI metadata before deployment.
rationale: 'When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization' (Lin & Gao, 2021, IEEE S&P) explicitly demonstrates that compiler optimizations break static signature recovery by eliminating the dispatch-pattern artifacts that tools like SigRec depend on. Neural-FEBI (He et al., 2023, JSS) addresses instruction reshuffling induced by compilers via a learned approach (bi-LSTM + CRF), suggesting that while dispatch-pattern heuristics are fragile, function boundary detection can be made robust via pattern learning. However, 'Building Reuse-Sensitive Control Flow Graphs for EVM Bytecode' (Wang et al., 2025) reveals that compilers introduce code-reuse patterns that create semantic ambiguities even in the CFG — a deeper structural problem than dispatch-pattern elimination. The key mechanistic claim is that optimization is an information-destroying channel: the source-level ABI signature is a tuple (name, param types) that gets mapped through selector hashing (collision-prone 32 bits) and then through optimization passes that may eliminate the only instructions revealing parameter usage. What remains is a strictly smaller information set.
supports_if: A cross-compiler-version study would show that ABI recovery accuracy (especially parameter-type recovery) is strongly predicted by optimization level (--optimize vs baseline) and compiler version, with method choice explaining relatively little residual variance. The 'When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization' paper already provides partial evidence: sig recovery accuracy drops significantly under optimization.
refutes_if: Any method achieves statistically indistinguishable ABI recovery accuracy on --optimize and --no-optimize-compiled contracts for the same source, demonstrating that it can recover information the compiler was believed to have destroyed. This would prove that the information is not truly lost but merely transformed into forms that the existing methods fail to exploit.
motivating_papers: When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization
Neural-FEBI: Accurate function identification in Ethereum Virtual Machine bytecode

hypothesis: The undecidability of precise jump-target resolution in EVM bytecode creates an inescapable precision–completeness tradeoff for all static ABI recovery methods: conservative overapproximation of jump targets preserves completeness (no missed functions) at the cost of precision (spurious function boundaries), while aggressive pruning preserves precision at the cost of completeness, and this tradeoff is fundamental — not an artifact of current tooling — because the problem reduces to solving the halting problem for the subset of contracts that compute jump destinations dynamically.
rationale: EVMLiSA (Arceri et al., 2025) and 'Towards a Sound Construction of EVM Bytecode Control-Flow Graphs' (Arceri et al., 2024) establish that sound CFG construction for EVM bytecode requires handling dynamic jumps where the target is stack-computed — a problem that is generally undecidable for arbitrary bytecode. Elipmoc (Grech et al., 2022) achieves 99.5% operand resolution through 'transactional sensitivity' — a form of context sensitivity that prunes infeasible paths — and path-sensitive argument/return inference, but this precision comes from aggressive pruning that may miss legitimate dynamic-call paths. Neural-FEBI (He et al., 2023) takes a different approach: a two-level bi-LSTM + CRF for function entry identification and control-flow traversal for boundary determination, achieving F1 88.3–99.7, but the low-end F1 (88.3) likely reflects contracts with dynamic dispatch patterns. 'Precise static modeling of Ethereum memory' (Lagouvardos et al., 2020) demonstrates that even when CFG structure is resolved, dynamic memory allocation patterns complicate high-level type recovery — a secondary precision–completeness tradeoff layered on top of the CFG one. The mechanistic claim is that these are the same tradeoff at different abstraction levels, both rooted in EVM's Turing-complete, stack-based execution model.
supports_if: Experiments show that the contracts on which different tools disagree are precisely those with the highest frequency of dynamic (computed) jump targets. A controlled study could measure: for each contract, count the number of unresolved jump targets, and show this count predicts the precision–completeness gap across all static tools (SigRec, Elipmoc, Neural-FEBI, EVMLiSA). SCDBench's finding that frontier LLMs perfectly decompile only 42/600 contracts is consistent with this fundamental limit — some contracts simply resist static analysis.
refutes_if: A static method is demonstrated that achieves both >99% precision AND >99% recall on function boundary identification across a representative corpus of contracts known to contain dynamically computed jump targets, with ground truth verified from source. This would prove that the undecidability of general jump-target resolution is not a practical barrier for real-world contracts.
